title: The Wanderings and the Manuscripts: a Name in Search of a Man
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Miner Flocker and the Road Out

stops.name: The German lands, the miner Flocker
stops.date_confidence: before 1473 by the narrative's own sequence, no year given; the text names no place at all, and the pin is the corpus's canonical Nuremberg borrowed as a placeholder for the German-speaking Empire, not a located site
stops.campa: A young man watches a miner work. Flocker digs ore and practises alchemy beside the digging, and he keeps what he knows behind his teeth. He fixes lead with a sulphur of his own, weighs twenty loth of the prepared lead against a mark of pure silver, and when the work is finished half the mark is gold. Then Flocker dies, and nobody can say what artifice he used. The young man has seen it happen. That is his entire capital: not a process, not a recipe, one afternoon of evidence that the thing can be done.
stops.quote: When I was a young fellow, I came to a Miner named Flocker, who was also an Alchemist, but he kept his knowledge secret, and I could get nothing out of him.
stops.quote_source: Trismosin's Alchemical Wanderings, in Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co., 1920), p. 82
suggested_refs: The opening page of Trismosin's Alchemical Wanderings, Kohn edition, 1920, p. 82
sources: Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (1920), p. 82, archive.org/stream/splendorsolisalc00tris

stops.name: The German lands, the road out in 1473
stops.date_confidence: the only year the narrative supplies, and every later chronology for Trismosin hangs on it; the departure point is unnamed and the pin stays at the Nuremberg placeholder
stops.campa: He counts eighteen months on the road and two hundred florins of his own money. He goes wherever he hears of an artist in alchemy, and each time he arrives he finds a man who can do one particular operation of no great importance, or a man who can do nothing at all. He learns the operations anyway. He watches the small true things work and the large claims fail, and he does not give up the search, because Flocker's half-gold mark of silver is still the fact against which every fraud gets measured.
stops.quote: As I had seen it really done by this miner, I started in the year 1473 on my travels to search out an artist in Alchemy, and where I heard of one I went to him, and in these wanderings I passed 18 months, learning all kinds of Alchemical Operations, of no great importance, but I saw the reality of some of the PARTICULAR processes, and I spent 200 Florins of my own money, nevertheless I would not give up the search.
stops.quote_source: Trismosin's Alchemical Wanderings, in Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (1920), p. 83
suggested_refs: The 1473 departure passage, Kohn edition, 1920, p. 83, the sole dated line in the autobiography

stops.name: Ljubljana, the turn south into Laibach
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the city is named in the text but no year is, and 1474 is counted forward from the eighteen months begun in 1473. The pin is the medieval town centre, since no street or house is given
stops.campa: Discouraged, and running out of the money he set out with, he turns south. Laibach lies on the road between the Empire and Italy, a town where a traveller from the German lands can still be understood and can still find a friend to board with. He does not stay. The plan, insofar as he has one, is Milan. The reasoning belongs to a man whose purse is thinner than his hope: go where the money and the libraries are, and where somebody might be paid to keep him while he looks.
suggested_refs: The old town square of Ljubljana, on the Empire-to-Italy road of the 1470s

stops.name: Milan, a year inside the monastery
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the house is not named, the year is inferred from the narrative sequence, and the pin sits at the historic centre as a placeholder for an unidentified monastery
stops.campa: At Milan he comes to a monastery, and for the first time since 1473 he stops moving. He hears excellent lectures. He serves as an assistant for about a year, which means fetching, tending, and doing whatever the house asks in exchange for a bed. The narrative names neither the monastery nor a teacher, and it claims not one transmutation for the whole of the year. It is the quietest passage in the wanderings, and the only one where the searcher lives like a student rather than a hunter.
suggested_refs: An unidentified Milanese monastery of the 1470s, the year of lectures

stops.name: Italy, fourteen weeks at the fire
stops.date_confidence: traditional; an itinerant phase with no fixed place named, the pin held at Milan where the leg begins. The year is a count forward through the narrative, not a date in it
stops.campa: Out of the monastery he goes up and down Italy, and falls in with two men who have solved his problem the practical way. An Italian tradesman and a German-speaking Jewish merchant know a corrosive process that turns English tin into something that passes for fine silver. He serves them fourteen weeks, tending the fire while they work, and he learns the process exactly. He has been searching three years for a real art and has been handed a counterfeit one, and he takes the wages it pays.
suggested_refs: The corrosive process for whitening English tin, learned over fourteen weeks at the furnace

stops.name: Venice, forty pounds sold to a Turk
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Saint Mark's Place is the only Venetian location this whole episode names, and the pin is set there. An earlier research pass placed the sale near the Rialto: that detail appears nowhere in the source and has been struck
stops.campa: He travels with the merchant to Venice. In the city of assayers and coin, before a Turkish merchant who has money to spend on bullion, forty pounds of the false silver change hands. The seller is confident and the buyer is satisfied. Trismosin stands at the edge of the transaction as the fire-tender who made the metal, watching a quantity of English tin walk away as treasure, and doing the only arithmetic that matters to him: if this is what he has learned, then he has learned nothing.
stops.quote: Then I journeyed with the Jew to Venice. There he sold to a Turkish merchant forty pounds of this Silver.
stops.quote_source: Trismosin's Alchemical Wanderings, in Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (1920), p. 83
suggested_refs: Piazza San Marco, the only Venetian site named in the counterfeit-silver sequence

stops.name: Venice, six loth carried to a goldsmith
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the shop is unlocated and the month is a narrative ordering, not a date. The pin sits at Saint Mark's Place, the square the text names as the goldsmith's referral
stops.campa: While the haggling goes on he takes six loth of the silver out of the parcel and carries it into a goldsmith's shop. The goldsmith speaks Latin, which is how the two of them can talk at all, and he does not test the metal himself. He sends the young German on to an assayer on Saint Mark's Place, where the furnaces are and where the guild's authority sits. It is a small act of private curiosity, taken behind the backs of the men paying his wages. He goes.
suggested_refs: The Latin-speaking goldsmith of Saint Mark's Place, unnamed in the source

stops.name: Venice, the cupel on Saint Mark's Place
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the premises are named only as an assayer's on Saint Mark's Place, and the month orders the narrative rather than dating it
stops.campa: The assayer is a wealthy man with three German assay-assistants at his benches. They put the six loth to the strong acids and then onto the cupel, in front of him, at heat. Nothing stands. The whole of it burns away and flies off in the fire, and the assistants speak harshly to the boy who brought it in. He answers that he only wanted to know whether it was real. He has his answer in the form he has wanted since Flocker died: not a claim, a test, and a result that cannot be argued with.
suggested_refs: The assay by cupellation on Saint Mark's Place, where the false silver flew away in the fire

stops.name: Venice, walking away from the fraud
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no place is given for the break, the pin is a city-centre placeholder, and the month orders the sequence only
stops.campa: He does not go back to the merchant. Venice hangs men for coining, and a foreign fire-tender attached to a parcel of false silver has no standing and no protector; his fear is entirely practical, and he says so. He drops the trade and the two men with it, and takes no further interest in their art. What he keeps is the address of the assayer's premises on Saint Mark's Place, and the memory of three German assistants who were employed there and handling real metal every day of the week.
stops.quote: When I saw the fraud, I returned not to the Jew, and paid no more attention to their art, for I feared to get into trouble together with the Jew, through the false silver.
stops.quote_source: Trismosin's Alchemical Wanderings, in Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (1920), p. 84
suggested_refs: Venetian statute against coining and the counterfeiting of bullion, the danger the narrator names

segments.name: The College, the Hospital, and Ponteleone

stops.name: Venice, two meals a day from the Rector
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the college is unnamed in the source and the pin is approximate to the city's central institutions. Tagged as reconstruction in the research pool because the house cannot be identified
stops.campa: With no wages and no trade he goes to a college in Venice and asks the Rector for two meals a day while he looks for work. The narrative gives no name for the house and no reason why a Rector should feed a stranger, only that he asks and is heard. This is the low point of the wanderings, three years out from the departure of 1473, and the man doing the asking is the same man who will shortly be handed a Greek manuscript worth six thousand crowns and told to make the process in it work.
suggested_refs: An unidentified Venetian college and its Rector, c. 1476

stops.name: Venice, the hospital of the foreign poor
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the institution is not named, and the pin is a city-centre placeholder. The common identification with the German foundations near the Fondaco dei Tedeschi is made by later readers, not by the text, and is carried here as unverified
stops.campa: The Rector sends him on to a hospital kept for destitute strangers, where Germans lodge alongside men of every nation passing through the port. He records one detail about the place and only one: the food is sumptuous. Venice feeds its foreign poor better than the Empire feeds its searchers. Later readers have tried to attach this house to the German charitable foundations near the Fondaco dei Tedeschi. The text attaches it to nothing, and that identification belongs to somebody else.
suggested_refs: Venetian hospitals for destitute foreign strangers in the later fifteenth century

stops.name: Ponteleone, recruited to the nobleman's laboratory
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Ponteleone matches no surviving toponym near Venice, and the pin is a placeholder on the terraferma at roughly the six Italian miles the text gives. Contradiction flagged: English Wikipedia puts Tauler at the Venice college instead, fusing two separate episodes, and the two accounts are not reconciled here
stops.campa: One of the three German assistants from the cupel comes looking for him. A Venetian nobleman keeps a laboratory at a mansion called Ponteleone, six Italian miles out of the city, and it needs hands. The terms are two crowns a week and board. The chief chemist is a German named Tauler, who knows how to fix mercury and will teach it. The man who a season ago was begging a Rector for two meals a day now has a bench, a salary, and the first genuine adept he has met since the miner died.
suggested_refs: Ponteleone, the unlocated mansion and laboratory six Italian miles from Venice

stops.name: Ponteleone, three loth of gold out of nine
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the year is a count forward through the narrative, and the site is the same unlocated placeholder
stops.campa: They test him before they trust him. He is given a cinnabar ore doctored with dirt, the sort of parcel that defeats a man working from a copied recipe, and told to get out what is in it. In two days he fixes the mercury. Nine loth go into the assay and three loth of fine gold come out. The nobleman rides out from the city without warning, speaks to him in Latin, calls him his Fortunatum, taps him on the shoulder, and gives him twenty-nine crowns on the spot.
stops.quote: That was my first work and stroke of luck. The Chief Chemist reported it to the nobleman, who came out unexpectedly, spoke to me in Latin, called me his Fortunatum, tapped me on the shoulder and gave me twenty-nine crowns.
stops.quote_source: Trismosin's Alchemical Wanderings, in Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (1920), p. 86
suggested_refs: The doctored cinnabar test at Ponteleone and the name Fortunatum

stops.name: Ponteleone, the oath of silence
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no date is given for the oath and the month orders the narrative only. The site remains the unlocated Ponteleone placeholder
stops.campa: Then they swear him. He is put on oath not to reveal the art to anyone, and the house closes around the work: everything kept secret, as the narrator holds it should be. His reasoning is not commercial. A man who boasts of his art, even holding the truth in his hands, will not be allowed by God's justice to go on. So the instruction he passes to whoever reads him has two unequal halves. Be silent, even with the highest tincture. Give charity, and let that be the part that shows.
stops.quote: I was then put on oath not to reveal my Art to anyone. To make a long story short, everything had to be kept secret, as it should be. If someone boasts of his art, even if he has got the Truth, God's Justice will not let such a one go on. Therefore be silent, even if you have the highest Tincture, but give charity.
stops.quote_source: Trismosin's Alchemical Wanderings, in Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (1920), p. 86
suggested_refs: The oath of secrecy sworn in the Ponteleone laboratory

stops.name: Ponteleone, six thousand crowns for the Sarlamethon
stops.date_confidence: traditional; undated in the source, ordered by the fifteen weeks the work is said to take. Correction carried from the research pool: the 6,000 crowns are additive to the 30,000 spent on books, not included in it
stops.campa: The nobleman has spent some thirty thousand crowns on alchemical books, and six thousand more, separately, on one Greek manuscript called Sarlamethon, a process for a tincture. Trismosin witnesses the payment. The text is translated and put into his hands to work, and in fifteen weeks he brings the process to a finish and tinges three metals into fine gold. No other document anywhere names the Sarlamethon. It exists in this sentence, at this price, and nowhere else that can be reached.
stops.quote: I myself witnessed that he paid 6,000 Crowns for the Manuscript SARLAMETHON. A process for a Tincture in the Greek Language. This the nobleman had soon translated and gave me to work. I brought that process to a finish in fifteen weeks. Therewith I tinged three metals into fine Gold; and this was kept most secret.
stops.quote_source: Trismosin's Alchemical Wanderings, in Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (1920), p. 86
suggested_refs: The Sarlamethon, a Greek tincture manuscript attested in this passage and nowhere else

stops.name: Venice, the Bucintoro leaves the Molo
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the ceremony falls on the movable feast of the Ascension and the year is counted through the narrative. The pin marks the Molo before the Doge's Palace, the attested departure point, correcting an earlier pass that placed the whole episode mid-basin
stops.campa: Once a year the Signoria goes out to wed the Adriatic. The Bucintoro casts off from the Molo in front of the Doge's Palace with the Doge aboard and the lords of the city following in their own vessels, and a ring goes into the water at the harbour mouth to make the marriage. The nobleman of Ponteleone takes his pleasure ship out with the rest. His laboratory is running with the chief chemist at the bench. The German who fixed the cinnabar is two years into his employment.
suggested_refs: The Bucintoro and the Sposalizio del Mare, departing annually from the Molo on Ascension Day

stops.name: Porto di Lido, the hurricane and the drowned nobleman
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the pin is the ceremony site off San Nicolo al Lido. Gap flagged: no Venetian civic record of this storm or this drowning has been checked, and the episode rests on the autobiography alone
stops.campa: Off San Nicolo al Lido, where the lagoon opens to the sea, a hurricane comes down on the ceremony of the Ascension. The nobleman drowns, and other lords of Venice drown with him in the same water. Within days the laboratory at Ponteleone is shut. The workers are counted out their wages and sent off, all but Tauler, and the German who fixed the cinnabar goes with them. Thirty-six thousand crowns of books and a Greek tincture proved in fifteen weeks now belong to a dead man.
suggested_refs: The Porto di Lido off San Nicolo, where the ring was cast and where the pleasure ships were caught

stops.name: Venice, leaving for a place he does not name
stops.date_confidence: the destination is a true gap: the text names no place, and this pin marks only the point of departure. Correction carried from the pool, which had him travelling onward to acquire the books; the construction is passive and the books are entrusted to him
stops.campa: He leaves Venice for somewhere he declines to name. There, Cabalistic and magical books in the Egyptian language are entrusted to his care; he does not go and fetch them, they are put into his hands. He has them carefully translated into Greek and then out of Greek into Latin, and in them he finds what he calls the Treasure of the Egyptians, with the names of the heathen kings of antiquity said to have held the tincture. The place has no name in the text. It never acquires one afterwards.
stops.quote: Then I went away from Venice, to a still better place for my purpose, where Cabalistic and Magical books in Egyptian language were entrusted to my care, these I had carefully translated into Greek, and then again retranslated into Latin. There I found and captured the Treasure of the Egyptians.
stops.quote_source: Trismosin's Alchemical Wanderings, in Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (1920), p. 87
suggested_refs: The unnamed 'still better place' of the Kohn text, p. 87, sometimes glossed as Egypt by later commentary the source does not support

stops.name: The unnamed place, a red no scarlet can match
stops.date_confidence: unlocated and undated; the pin repeats the Venice departure point because the source supplies no other, and the year is a count forward from the closing of the laboratory
stops.campa: After a while he sees the fundamental principles of the art, and begins working out the best tincture. At the end of the work there is a red that no scarlet can be compared with, and a treasure he says words cannot tell, which can be augmented without limit. One part tinges fifteen hundred parts of silver into gold. The last thing that happens in the narrative is this: an unnamed man, in an unnamed place, in an unrecorded year, holding up a colour.
stops.quote: After a while I saw the fundamental principles of this art, then I began working out the Best Tincture... when I came to the end of the Work I found such a beautiful red colour as no scarlet can compare with, and such a treasure as words cannot tell, and which can be infinitely augmented. One part tinged 1,500 parts Silver into Gold.
stops.quote_source: Trismosin's Alchemical Wanderings, in Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (1920), pp. 87-88
suggested_refs: The final tincture passage, straddling pp. 87-88 of the Kohn edition

stops.name: The unnamed place, the verse that ends the wanderings
stops.date_confidence: unlocated and undated; the pin and the year carry over from the previous stop. Everything in the traditional biography after this point comes from other hands, not from the narrative
stops.campa: The wanderings end in a verse, printed in capitals, that turns the travel narrative inside out. Everything the reader has followed, the miner, the counterfeit silver, the cupel, Ponteleone, the Egyptian books, resolves into an instruction addressed to whoever is holding the book: what you know of this art is what you are, and all that is outside you is also within. Then the text signs itself with the name, and the man who was walking through Italy becomes a doctrine.
stops.quote: STUDY WHAT THOU ART, WHEREOF THOU ART A PART, WHAT THOU KNOWEST OF THIS ART, THIS IS REALLY WHAT THOU ART. ALL THAT IS WITHOUT THEE ALSO IS WITHIN. THUS WROTE TRISMOSIN.
stops.quote_source: Closing verse of Trismosin's Alchemical Wanderings, in Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (1920), p. 88
suggested_refs: The closing verse of the Wanderings, the only place in the narrative where the name signs itself

stops.name: Einsiedeln, the tutors who were never there
stops.date_confidence: no source of any kind places Trismosin here; this stop records an absence. The pin is inherited byte-identical from johannes_trithemius.journey.json, whose own Einsiedeln stop flags the schooling legend as unsubstantiated
stops.campa: Einsiedeln keeps the birth-house of Paracelsus and a legend that he was schooled here under four bishops and under Trithemius, a claim recorded and rejected in the same breath by Trithemius's own documented life. The slot is open, and legends fill open slots. No source reached, here or elsewhere, places Trismosin at Einsiedeln, in the abbey school or anywhere near it. The pin marks the shape of a story that was never told about him, and the absence stands rather than being filled.
suggested_refs: The Einsiedeln schooling legend as caveated in johannes_trithemius.journey.json, 'Einsiedeln, the tutors who were never there'

stops.name: Wurzburg, the rival claimant
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Paracelsus and Trithemius tutelage, and pinned byte-identical to both corpus files; Trismosin's rival claim to the same role carries no date and no document, and is recorded as tradition standing beside tradition
stops.campa: In April 1508 the boy Theophrastus is sent to Wurzburg to sit with Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the Schottenkloster and the greatest master of the hidden sciences in the Empire. The tutelage is recorded at this pin, alongside a rival claimant: Salomon Trismosin, also called his teacher. Both traditions stand and neither is settled. Trithemius has charters, two thousand books, and a grave in the Neumunster. The rival has a title page.
stops.quote: The queue holds a rival claimant besides, Salomon Trismosin, also called his teacher. Both traditions stand, and neither is settled here.
stops.quote_source: johannes_trithemius.journey.json, stop 'Wurzburg, the abbot and the secret art', 1508-04-01
suggested_refs: The Schottenkloster St. Jakob at Wurzburg, where the corpus places the documented tutelage

stops.name: Constantinople, the meeting with Paracelsus
stops.date_confidence: legendary; asserted as fact by English Wikipedia citing Patai 1994, unattested in any Paracelsian source consulted, and dissolved outright by the 2019 Watkins volume, which treats Trismosin as a construct of Paracelsus's followers. The pin is inherited byte-identical from paracelsus.journey.json
stops.campa: Paracelsus travels east between 1517 and 1524, and Constantinople is on the list of places he goes. The tradition puts Trismosin there in 1520, teaching him the art. Nothing Paracelsus wrote names Trismosin. Nothing credited to Trismosin mentions Paracelsus; the wanderings had already closed in an unnamed place forty years earlier and never resume. The meeting lives in a third place, in the literature that grew around both names, placed here where that literature puts it.
suggested_refs: Raphael Patai, The Jewish Alchemists (1994), the source English Wikipedia cites for the meeting; not consulted in this pass

stops.name: Galata, the quarter where the strangers lodge
stops.date_confidence: no site within the city is named in any source; Galata is a plausible district for a European traveller and nothing more, and the month is an ordering device. The pin sits at the Galata Tower
stops.campa: No source names a street, a house, a khan, or a quarter for the meeting. Galata is where the Europeans of the city keep their consulates and their credit, and where they lodge their travellers, so Galata is where a wandering German adept would be looked for. That is the entire basis of this pin. It is a plausible district standing in for an attested address that does not exist, in a city that enters the Trismosin story only because a later tradition needed somewhere far enough away.
suggested_refs: The Galata quarter of Ottoman Constantinople, residence of European merchants and travellers

stops.name: Nuremberg, the circle of rumour
stops.date_confidence: attested for the corpus events pinned here, 1529 and 1532; no Trismosin presence in Nuremberg is claimed by any source, and the stop records the contrast
stops.campa: Nuremberg is where Paracelsus first signs the adopted name in 1529, and where in 1532 the council refuses Johann Faust safe conduct through the gates. The city keeps a register of who is let in and who is turned away, a register this account keeps returning to for that exact reason: Nuremberg writes things down. Trismosin appears in no Nuremberg record of any kind. A copy of the Splendor Solis will reach the city eventually. The man never does.
suggested_refs: Nuremberg council records of safe conduct, 1532, and the corpus stops at this pin in paracelsus.journey.json and johann_faust.journey.json

stops.name: Basel, where the table talk gets printed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the corpus events at this pin, 1527-1563; the Trismosin connection is structural and no source places him or his printers in Basel
stops.campa: Basel is where Paracelsus lectures in German, cures Froben, and burns Avicenna in 1527, and where twenty years later Johann Gast writes down the table talk that seeds the Faust legend. When this circle turns from a life into a story it usually happens here, in a printing town with a university and men who take notes at dinner. No printer in Basel handles Trismosin. His transmission runs instead through manuscripts nobody signs, and then one press on the Bodensee, seventy years later.
suggested_refs: Johann Gast's Basel table talk and the Basel stops of paracelsus.journey.json and johann_faust.journey.json

stops.name: Augsburg, seven chapters or seven treatises
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a live contradiction. English Wikipedia gives the Augsburg origin in one uncited sentence with no date; German scholarship dates the text c. 1440 in Middle Low German and attributes it to Ulrich Poyssel, with no Augsburg at all. The year follows the dated reading, the pin follows the placed one, and neither is adjudicated
stops.campa: English Wikipedia gives the Splendor Solis an origin at Augsburg in a shorter form of seven chapters, in one sentence, with no date and no citation attached to it. German scholarship gives the text a Middle Low German origin around 1440, in seven treatises, and attributes it to Ulrich Poyssel, with no Augsburg in the account anywhere. The two readings do not overlap in language, in structure, or in place. The city one of them names is where the pin sits, the other account left unresolved.
suggested_refs: The uncited Augsburg sentence in English Wikipedia's 'Splendor Solis', set against the German article's c. 1440 Poyssel attribution

stops.name: Berlin, the oldest illuminated copy
stops.date_confidence: contested. German Wikipedia's census gives the manuscript as Nuremberg 1531 and dates the oldest surviving version 1531-1532 in Middle Low German; English Wikipedia gives Central German, 1532-1535. Year and dialect are both disputed and the file carries the earlier dating without settling it
stops.campa: The oldest illuminated copy that survives is a small painted book: twenty-two allegorical plates on vellum, gold-heightened borders in the manner of a book of hours, miniatures working in the visual language of Durer, Holbein, and Cranach. It carries the name Trismosin, and it is more than sixty years older than any printing of that name. The Kupferstichkabinett at the Kulturforum holds it as MS 78 D 3. This object, and not a person, is the earliest hard evidence the subject has.
suggested_refs: Kupferstichkabinett, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, MS 78 D 3, the earliest extant illuminated Splendor Solis

stops.name: London, Harley MS 3469
stops.date_confidence: attested as circa 1582, German work, British Library catalogue. Note against an earlier pass: this is not in contradiction with the Berlin dating, since Berlin and Harley are two different manuscripts
stops.campa: Harley MS 3469, made in Germany about 1582, is the copy the world actually sees. Its plates are the ones reproduced in every later book on alchemical imagery: the sun over the city, the knight at the fountain, the seven flasks of the planets inside the fourth treatise, the black sun rising over a river. The British Library holds it. Half a century after Berlin, the manuscript tradition is still copying itself by hand, and still setting the same name at the head of the text.
suggested_refs: British Library, Harley MS 3469, the most reproduced Splendor Solis

stops.name: Kassel, two copies in one library
stops.date_confidence: undated; neither Kassel manuscript carries a date in the reachable census, and 1600 is a placeholder that carries no evidential weight. The pin is the Murhardsche Bibliothek, where the historic collections are kept
stops.campa: Kassel holds two of them, Ms. chem. 11 and Ms. chem. 21, kept with the historic collections of the university library at the Murhardsche on Bruder-Grimm-Platz. Two copies in one provincial library measures how the text moved: not through a market, but through the private cabinets of men who wanted the pictures and the process together. About twenty copies survive worldwide. Nobody has established which is copied from which, and neither Kassel manuscript carries a date.
suggested_refs: Universitatsbibliothek Kassel, Ms. chem. 11 and Ms. chem. 21, at the Murhardsche Bibliothek

stops.name: Paris, a copy and no shelfmark
stops.date_confidence: undated and unverified; the source gives only the city. The pin sits at the Richelieu site of the Bibliotheque nationale as the likeliest repository, and 1600 is a placeholder year with no evidential weight
stops.campa: A copy is in Paris. That is the whole of what the reachable sources say. The pin sits at the Richelieu site of the Bibliotheque nationale because that is where such a manuscript would be, not because a catalogue record was found for it. Neither the English list nor the German census gives it a shelfmark. A text whose entire claim to a historical author rests on its manuscript tradition has no full catalogue of that tradition in anything reachable here. The list of survivals is a list of cities.
suggested_refs: An uncatalogued Paris copy of the Splendor Solis, library and shelfmark unconfirmed

stops.name: Nuremberg, a copy in the city the census names
stops.date_confidence: undated and unverified; repository not confirmed, and the pin sits at the Germanisches Nationalmuseum as a plausible keeper. 1600 is a placeholder with no evidential weight
stops.campa: A copy is in Nuremberg, the city the German census also names in its dating of the Berlin manuscript: Nuremberg 1531. Whether the surviving Nuremberg copy has anything to do with that dating is established nowhere reachable. The pin sits at the Germanisches Nationalmuseum, the city's principal keeper of manuscripts. Like Paris, this is an entry in a list of survivals rather than a located and catalogued book, and it sits two kilometres from the council that turned Faust away.
suggested_refs: Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Nuremberg, as plausible repository of the listed Nuremberg copy

stops.name: Rorschach, Leonhard Straub sets the type
stops.date_confidence: attested from the 1598 imprint, printer named. Contradiction flagged: German Wikipedia gives 1599 for the Rorschach printing. The work appeared in parts across 1598-1599, so 1598 for the first is defensible and is what the file carries
stops.campa: At Rorschach on the Bodensee, Leonhard Straub prints Aureum vellus, oder, Guldin Schatz und Kunstkammer. The title is Latin and everything under it is German. Bound into the collection are the Splendor Solis, in print for the first time, and a first-person travel narrative in which a man named Salomon Trismosin says he set out in 1473. A hundred and twenty-five years after that claimed departure, in a lake town of a few thousand souls, the subject of this journey acquires a documented existence.
suggested_refs: Aureum vellus, oder, Guldin Schatz und Kunstkammer, Rorschach: Leonhard Straub, 1598, archive.org/details/aureumvellusoder01tris

stops.name: Rome, the Index that never came
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Steganographia listing of 1609 at this pin; the Trismosin entry here is a recorded absence, since no Index history for the Splendor Solis or the Aureum Vellus was found in any reachable source
stops.campa: Rome is where the fate of dangerous books gets decided. Trithemius's Steganographia goes onto the Index in 1609 and comes off it in 1900. The Splendor Solis never goes on, and neither does the Aureum Vellus. A German book of transmutation, printed in a Protestant lake town, full of pictures of dismemberment and resurrection and a black sun over a river, passes three centuries without attracting a censor. This pin records what did not happen to it, which is a fact of the same kind.
suggested_refs: Index Librorum Prohibitorum, 1609 and 1900, the Steganographia entries recorded in johannes_trithemius.journey.json

stops.name: Paris, the translator who signs two letters
stops.date_confidence: attested from the 1612 imprint, Paris. Correction carried: an earlier pass reported no place of production for this translation. The pin is the canonical corpus Paris, inherited byte-identical, rather than a printing-quarter address
stops.campa: La Toyson d'or, ou la fleur des thresors appears at Paris, translated out of the German by a man who signs himself L. I. and nothing more. The engravings are fine and some copies are coloured by hand. Fourteen years after Rorschach the book has crossed a language and a border and become an object for collectors, and the anonymity has doubled: an author who is a pseudonym, now carried into French by a translator who is two letters and a full stop.
suggested_refs: La Toyson d'or, ou la fleur des thresors, Paris, 1612, archive.org/details/latoysondorovlaf00tris

stops.name: Oxford, the Golden Fleece in Ashmole's library
stops.date_confidence: seventeenth century, exact year unknown: no date for Backhouse's translation was found in any reachable source, and 1650 is a placeholder inside his working life. Custody is attested, not inferred, since two thirds of Ashmole's library passed to the Bodleian
stops.campa: William Backhouse turns the French into English and calls it The Golden Fleece. The manuscript survives as Ashmole MS 1395, part of Elias Ashmole's library, two thirds of which came to the Bodleian when the Victorians separated the books from the museum collection. No date is recorded for the translation. Backhouse is the Berkshire alchemist who took Ashmole as his adopted son and told him the secret on what he thought was his deathbed. That is the circle the text lands in.
suggested_refs: Bodleian Library, Ashmole MS 1395, William Backhouse's English Golden Fleece

stops.name: Paris, the Frenchman who saw him alive
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction with no support: Hartmann gives no place, no year beyond the end of the century, and no source. The pin is the canonical corpus Paris, standing in for the traveller's nationality, and it locates nothing
stops.campa: Franz Hartmann, writing in the 1890s, reports that a French traveller saw Trismosin alive at the end of the seventeenth century, and adds that his real name was Pfeiffer. He gives no source for either statement. The arithmetic is the point rather than an embarrassment: a man travelling as an adult in 1473 and seen alive in the 1690s has lived past two hundred years, which is what possession of the elixir would look like from outside. The traveller is not named. Neither is the place.
suggested_refs: Franz Hartmann's late nineteenth-century alchemical writings, source of the sighting and of the name Pfeiffer

stops.name: Salzburg, the grave that exists for the other man
stops.date_confidence: the date is that of the monument raised over Paracelsus at Sankt Sebastian; Trismosin carries no date here because he has no grave, no memorial, and no death record anywhere in the reachable sources
stops.campa: At Sankt Sebastian in Salzburg there is a stone over Paracelsus and a monument raised by people who wanted somewhere to stand. At the Neumunster in Wurzburg there is a grave for Trithemius. For Trismosin there is nothing: no tomb, no memorial, no parish register, no death notice, no town that claims him. Of Paracelsus's three claimed teachers, two have a grave that can be visited. The third has a title page, twenty manuscripts scattered across five cities, and a printed voice.
suggested_refs: The Paracelsus monument at Sankt Sebastian, Salzburg, and the Trithemius grave at the Neumunster, Wurzburg

stops.name: London, Kegan Paul prints him in English
stops.date_confidence: attested, 1920 imprint. The pin is a London centroid for the publisher rather than a verified street address for Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co.
stops.campa: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner of London print an English Splendor Solis with the twenty-two plates and the Wanderings appended, translated by Julius Kohn, who signs himself J.K. This is the edition every English quotation of Trismosin has come through since, including all ten quoted here. Kohn is candid at the close of his own commentary about what he has been editing: the origin of the writings is uncertain, and he thinks most of what carries the name is spurious or has been tampered with.
stops.quote: The origin of the writings attributed to Trismosin is uncertain and wrapped in mystery.
stops.quote_source: J.K., editorial commentary under the running head 'Trismosin's Alchemical Process', in Splendor Solis (London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co., 1920), p. 95
suggested_refs: Splendor Solis: Alchemical Treatises of Solomon Trismosin, trans. J.K., 1920, the source of every English quotation in this file
sources: Splendor Solis, trans. J.K. (1920), p. 95, archive.org/stream/splendorsolisalc00tris

stops.name: London, the hundred and fifty years
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction at second hand: the 1617 Elucidarius Chymicus was not fetched, and the claim is known only through Kohn's 1920 paraphrase of its preface. The pin marks that edition, not the 1617 imprint, whose place of printing was not established
stops.campa: In the same closing pages Kohn passes on a claim from the preface of the Elucidarius Chymicus of 1617, a book not consulted directly here and known only at second hand: that Trismosin lived by virtue of his medicine to the age of one hundred and fifty. He adds that Schmieder believed the name was Pfeifer and the man a Saxon. Two centuries after Schmieder's guess, Hartmann will offer Pfeiffer with a second f and two hundred years instead of one fifty, and cite nobody at all.
stops.quote: Of Trismosin, whose name Schmieder believes to have been Pfeifer, and that he was a Saxon, it is related in the Preface to the book 'Elucidarius Chymicus, 1617' that he lived by virtue of (or perhaps, despite) his Medicine to an age of ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY YEARS!
stops.quote_source: J.K., in Splendor Solis (London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co., 1920), p. 95, reporting the preface to Elucidarius Chymicus (1617)
suggested_refs: Elucidarius Chymicus (1617), preface, not fetched in this pass and known only through Kohn's report of it

stops.name: London, Watkins dissolves the author
stops.date_confidence: attested publication, Watkins 2019, ISBN 9781786782595. Weakest link flagged: the volume itself was not read, and the Poysel correction rests on the publisher's description and Prinke's chapter title alone
stops.campa: Watkins of London publish Splendor Solis: The World's Most Famous Alchemical Manuscript, by Skinner, Prinke, Hedesan and Godwin. Prinke's chapter sets out the reasons for the misattribution of the work to Poysel and to Trismosin. English Wikipedia reads that volume backwards and reports Skinner as proposing the Poysel identification the book argues against. The scholarship dissolves the author, the encyclopaedia reconstitutes him, and both operations sit recorded at one pin.
suggested_refs: Skinner, Prinke, Hedesan and Godwin, Splendor Solis: The World's Most Famous Alchemical Manuscript (Watkins, 2019), ISBN 9781786782595
sources: Watkins Publishing, 2019, volume description and chapter listing
